questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Described experiences of the different study environment, my girlfriend living there, the much more hands-on approach to teaching.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Somewhat easy, the people from the International Office at UvA were very nice and even held a personal call with me to make sure I knew what to do on my first days. Information about Erasmus and the general framework of the program and the conditions on the other hand was very hard to find. I would have wished to be informed about things like minimal requirements beforehand.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The people from the International Office at UvA were very nice and even held a personal call with me to make sure I knew what to do on my first days. They also regularly sent me emails for important matters to make sure I knew what to do.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Very easy, the uni gave me an application to fill out and since I did it very early I did get a flat. Be warned though, the places go very quickly and finding private accomodation in Amsterdam is an absolutely horrendous experience.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: The public transport system of Amsterdam is incredibly good. Make sure to get an OV-Chipkaart so you can use any train and bus anywhere in the Netherlands without any problems.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I got sent a link where I had to fill in my personal details and the uni did the rest for me. They even handled all my immigration matters for me.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I could always contact the international student office.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
Very unsuccessful. To be frank, registering for courses was a bit of a disaster. Since my degree (Computer Science) is a joint degree between the two universities in Amsterdam, Vrije Universiteit and the Universiteit van Amsterdam, half of the courses are from the different uni. I was told that as an exchange student you are not allowed to take any courses from the other university, which barred me from four of my five selected courses already. There were also capacity restraints which barred me from taking further courses. This left me with basically a predetermined choice of courses I could take.

I also later found out that other exchange students were in fact allowed to take courses from the other university, so I am not sure what is the deciding factor there...

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Do it as soon as possible. In basically anything the dutch have a policy of first-come-first-serve.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Some courses were on an adequate level compared to UCPH courses, some were adequate had they correctly assessed the required previous knowledge. Because they didn't I took courses that I lacked quite a lot of prerequisite knowledge for.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Teaching is much more personal and practical. Courses are rarely bigger than 50 people and I had courses as small as 13 people. The content of the courses is also much more focused on immediately applying learned knowledge rather than theoretical practice.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Programming Multi- and Many Core Systems (PMMS), DevOps and Cloud-based Software, Type Theory, Computational Biology, Climate Change

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
PMMS is great, it is very hands-on and the professors are very enthusiastic. Unfortunately the communication for the final exam was basically nonexistent, leading almost my entire assignment group to fail the exam because they prepared for other things than were asked for in the exam. DevOps is also very fun and the professors are very enthusiastic. The course is basically a project. Computational Biology and Type Theory seem like decent courses, but I lacked a lot of prerequisite knowledge, making it hard for me to follow the courses or judge on their quality.
Climate Change was the single best course I have ever had at a university. The professor is incredibly enthusiastic and passionate both about the subject and teaching the content to the students. Unfortunately, this was the last time the course was held, though, as the professor is now going into retirement.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: The city of Amsterdam will charge you ~260€ (~2000DKK) for garbage disposal fees for an entire year.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Transportation was cheaper than expected, with a bike you have basically zero transportation costs and bikes are incredibly cheap.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Cannot really say as I did not use any of it, but the UvA has a massive sports offering for students.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go around town on Kings Day, the entire city turns into a festival. There are some amazing bouldering gyms in Amsterdam as well.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
De Grote Veluwe is a national park in the center of the netherlands, it's super beautiful and has an art museum at the center. The entire park can (in classic dutch fashion) be travelled by bikes which are free at the entrance.
Zandvoort is a lovely town at the coast. It is also worthwhile to visit the rest of the big cities in the Netherlands at least once, like Den Haag and Rotterdam.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Super easy. Dutch people are very friendly.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Find something outside of university to bond with Dutch people. Dutch students usually stick to Dutch students at uni, so it is easier to make contact with them outside of university.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None, really.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The hate for bureaucracy most dutch people have is a blessing since it simplifies a lot of things to not have to follow much bureaucracy. This also leads to some funny situations, though, where for example there is no official process to deregister from an exam, you just talk to the professor about it.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1) Find housing through the Uni, housing in Amsterdam is worse than in Copenhagen. 2) Make sure the courses you choose actually fit your skills 3) Enjoy yourself!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: You can apply for housing support with the dutch government. It is called "Huurtoeslag" in dutch.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting many different people, living in another country and learning the language

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Managing my courses and following courses with too little previous knowledge

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
